strengths: Original and technically well-motivated formulation: replacing loss-based 'learnability' with a metric-aligned, image-level estimate of the marginal contribution to dataset-level mAP (DetGain) directly addresses a real limitation of applying generic data-selection signals to detection, where losses are fragmented across classification/localization/assignment terms.

The derivation of the marginal ΔAP via a Stieltjes-integral formulation in the score-threshold domain (Eqs. 6–9) and its closed-form reduction under a uniform Beta(1,1) prior (Eqs. 25–26) is elegant, gives O(1) per-detection cost, and is empirically validated against Monte Carlo simulation (Fig. 5) with excellent agreement — this is a genuine technical contribution beyond simple heuristics.

The method is architecture-agnostic and post-hoc (operates only on prediction outputs, no loss/architecture changes), which is convincingly demonstrated across six detectors spanning one-stage, two-stage, anchor-free, and transformer families, all showing consistent mAP gains (~+2.0 average).

Thorough ablation suite: teacher backbone size (Table 3), sampling ratio/accuracy-cost trade-off (Table 4), joint effect of augmentation + sampling (Table 2, Table 10), and comparison against seven alternative online sampling metrics (Table 5), including the recent image-wise AP approach.

Strong and well-documented robustness under annotation noise (Fig. 4) and pseudo-labels (Appendix 2), where the advantage over loss-based baselines grows with noise level — an important practical property.
Clear complementarity with knowledge distillation (Table 6) and evidence of accelerated convergence (Fig. 7), plus a clear, reproducible implementation recipe (Algorithm 1, Listing 1, MMDetection).

The paper is generally well written, with a clear problem statement, careful positioning relative to active learning, offline coreset selection, and architecture-coupled sampling methods, and it honestly acknowledges limitations.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single dataset (COCO). No results on other detection benchmarks (e.g., LVIS, Objects365, or a domain-specific set), so the generality of the ~+2 mAP gains is not fully established.

Training cost is roughly 2.5× wall-clock due to the super-batch scoring; the paper acknowledges this but does not report an equal-compute/equal-wall-clock baseline comparison (e.g., training the uniform baseline for the same number of iterations/wall-clock), which is the standard fairness check in data-selection work and would materially strengthen the efficiency claim.

No variance/seed reporting. All results appear to be single runs, and gains are modest (+1.6 to +2.7 mAP), so statistical significance of the improvements (and of the metric ranking in Table 5) is unclear.

The central design choice — the uniform prior — is justified mainly empirically (Table 11) and by convenience; the theoretical argument that a maximum-entropy prior preserves the correct sample ordering is plausible but not rigorously established, and the approximation error introduced by the uniform-prior closed form relative to true ΔmAP is not quantified beyond the Monte Carlo check on synthetic distributions.

The teacher-student design requires a pretrained teacher from the same architecture family with a stronger backbone to get the best gains (Appendix 1 shows cross-family teachers are weaker); this constrains applicability and adds an implicit dependency on the availability of a suitable teacher.

The contribution relative to the closely related image-wise AP selection method (Zhou et al., 2024, ref [61]) could be articulated more sharply — the reported improvement over it in Table 5 is small (e.g., 40.0 vs 39.4 AP for Faster R-CNN), so the incremental value of the global-AP framing over per-image AP is not strongly separated from noise.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: online, per-image data curation for object detection, where loss-based learnability signals from classification/contrastive learning are known to be unreliable due to fragmented, sampling-dependent detection losses.

The core idea—defining learnability as the teacher–student gap in each image's estimated marginal contribution to dataset-level mAP (DetGain), rather than in raw loss—is clean, well motivated, and metric-aligned. Deriving an analytic, closed-form ΔAP under a uniform TP/FP score prior (Eqs. 25–26) makes per-image scoring O(1) per detection and model-agnostic, avoiding reliance on architecture-specific internals (RPN sampling, Hungarian matching, etc.).

The theoretical development is rigorous and well supported: the Stieltjes-integral derivation of single-insertion ΔAP, the decomposition into self-contribution and precision-reweighting terms, and the class/IoU aggregation (Eq. 9) are clearly laid out, and the Monte Carlo verification in Appendix 4 (Fig. 5) shows excellent agreement with the analytic solution, which is good scientific practice.

Broad and thorough empirical evaluation: six representative detectors (Faster R-CNN, ATSS, FCOS, GFL, VFNet, Deformable DETR) on COCO, consistent gains of roughly +1.6 to +2.7 mAP, plus ablations on teacher backbone, sampling ratio/overhead, augmentation, comparison against seven alternative sampling metrics (Table 5), robustness to annotation noise (Fig. 4), pseudo-label noise (Table 8), and complementarity with knowledge distillation (Table 6).

The pairing of DetGain subsampling with strong online augmentation is a sensible and empirically validated design: Table 2 shows that learnability-only sampling overfits while augmentation-only gives limited gains, and the combination restores diversity and yields the best generalization. The mechanism is plausibly explained via the enlarged augmented sampling space (Fig. 3).

Practical, non-intrusive deployment: the method modifies only the data pipeline, leaves architecture, loss, and inference latency unchanged, and is validated as architecture-agnostic across one/two-stage and transformer detectors, with framework-agnostic pseudocode provided (Listing 1).
Clear writing and organization; limitations (training-time overhead, naive augmentation, potential for more adaptive strategies) are explicitly acknowledged rather than hidden.
weaknesses: The reported gains, while consistent, are modest (≈+2.0 mAP average), and some individual improvements (e.g., GFL +1.6/+1.8, VFNet +1.9/+2.0) are within the range where single-run COCO variance is a concern. No error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported, so the robustness of the headline numbers cannot be fully assessed.

The training-cost overhead is substantial: Table 4 indicates roughly ×2.4–2.5 wall-clock for the chosen 20% sampling ratio, and the paper notes additional forward passes through both teacher and student for scoring. The paper frames this as an acceptable offline investment, but for a data-efficiency method this trade-off deserves more direct discussion (e.g., mAP per unit compute vs. baselines).

The uniform Beta(1,1) prior is a strong simplifying assumption. Under it, the DetGain for a TP is monotone increasing in score and for an FP monotone decreasing, so the resulting ranking is effectively a monotone surrogate for detection-quality/confidence aggregated over classes and IoU thresholds, rather than a calibrated marginal mAP. Table 11 further shows the model-specific prior gives negligible validation gain, which raises the question of whether simpler heuristics (e.g., mean matched IoU, mean confidence of matched TPs) would perform comparably. Such baselines are not compared against.

The additive approximation δmAP(B) ≈ Σ δmAP(x) ignores interactions among detections within an image (NMS, duplicate/competing boxes, ranking interdependencies) and treats detections independently; the paper bounds the error only by O(|B|/|D|) and does not empirically probe how much this matters at realistic batch sizes.

The comparison against prior online curation is indirect. Table 5 compares against proxy variants (loss-learnability, Image-AP [61], entropy-based metrics) run in the authors' own framework rather than against the original RHO-LOSS [37], JEST [14], or ACED [49] pipelines as published, so the claim that DetGain is uniquely effective among online curators is not fully established.

The related-work framing ('few studies have demonstrated tangible performance gains' for online detection sampling) is somewhat strong given existing metric-driven selection work such as [61], which the method explicitly generalizes; the precise incremental novelty relative to that line of work could be delineated more sharply.

The noise-injection protocol (random label swaps, box jitter, fake-box addition) is one plausible corruption model, but real-world label noise often has structure (e.g., class confusion, systematic annotation bias); the robustness conclusion may not transfer fully.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and genuinely underexplored problem: online data curation for object detection, where generic learnability metrics do not transfer cleanly due to fragmented losses and ranking-based evaluation.

Provides an analytic closed-form for the marginal change in dataset-level mAP from inserting a single TP or FP (Eqs. 25–26), with a Monte Carlo verification (Appendix 4, Fig. 5) demonstrating correctness and numerical stability of the derivation.

The design is largely plug-and-play and detector-agnostic in principle, modifying only the data pipeline rather than the loss, architecture, or training schedule, and the paper supplies algorithm/pseudocode for reproducibility.

Experimental breadth is good: six representative detectors spanning two-stage, one-stage, and transformer families, plus ablations on augmentation, teacher capacity, sampling ratio, and noise robustness (Tables 1–5, Figs. 4, 7).

Demonstrates practical robustness under annotation noise and pseudo-labels and shows complementarity with knowledge distillation (Tables 6, 8), which are useful empirical findings beyond the headline mAP.
weaknesses: The central technical simplification—assuming uniform (Beta(1,1)) TP/FP score distributions—collapses the closed-form DetGain into a fixed monotonic function of each detection's confidence score (Eqs. 25–26 depend only on s and global T, F). The image-level signal thus reduces to a confidence-weighted sum, yet the paper never ablates whether this machinery is needed versus a trivial score-sum or confidence heuristic, so the value of the 'marginal AP contribution' framing is not isolated.

Table 2 is a serious red flag for the core premise: online sampling alone (no augmentation) actually lowers validation AP (37.3 vs. 37.4 baseline), and the gains only materialize when combined with strong augmentation (39.9). This suggests the claimed DetGain signal is not itself identifying useful samples and that the reported benefit is an entanglement/synergy with augmentation that the paper does not disentangle.

In the controlled comparison against the closest competitors (Table 5, with augmentation applied to all methods), DetGain improves over loss-learnability by only ~1.1 mAP (38.9→40.0) and over Image-AP by ~1.6. The headline '+2.0–2.7 mAP' is measured against a weaker baseline, overstating the practical margin over prior art.

Novelty is incremental. Teacher–student 'learnability' is directly inherited from RHO-LOSS (Mindermann et al.), and the main new element is the AP-marginal re-derivation for detection. The paper does not sufficiently articulate what is conceptually new beyond porting an existing selection principle to a new task with a metric-aware score.

The 'architecture-agnostic / plug-and-play' claim is weakened by the need for a same-family teacher (Appendix 1/Table 7 shows asymmetric teachers degrade gains) and by per-detector-family augmentation tuning (Table 10), which is hand-tuned engineering rather than a general recipe.

The method incurs substantial extra compute (~2.5–3× pre-selection wall-clock, Table 4 and Section 4.3) with no comparison to cheaper detection-specific selection heuristics, and the cost/benefit trade-off is asserted rather than carefully quantified against simpler alternatives.

Minor inconsistencies in reported numbers (e.g., Faster R-CNN +Data Aug AP of 37.5 in Table 1 vs. the 37.3 uniform baseline in Table 5) reduce confidence in the exact magnitudes, and the uniform-prior justification via maximum entropy is a convenience argument rather than a demonstrated property of real detector score distributions.

strengths: The paper introduces DetGain, a novel metric-aware online data curation framework for object detection that estimates each image's marginal contribution to dataset-level mAP, filling a gap where generic learnability metrics (loss-based) fail due to the fragmented and architecture-dependent nature of detection losses.

The mathematical formulation is rigorous and well-founded: the authors derive an analytic closed-form expression for the marginal ΔAP of inserting a single TP/FP detection (Eqs. 7-8), which under a uniform prior simplifies to compact forms (Eqs. 10, 25-26). These derivations are carefully verified via Monte Carlo simulation (Appendix 4, Fig. 7), showing near-perfect agreement between simulated and analytic ΔAP across detectors.

The method is genuinely architecture-agnostic and plug-and-play: it only queries standard predict() interfaces and does not modify model architectures, loss functions, or optimizers, as demonstrated across six representative detectors spanning two-stage, one-stage anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based families (Table 1).

Experiments are extensive and well-controlled: comparisons against six alternative sampling metrics (Table 4), robustness to annotation noise and pseudo-labels (Fig. 5, Appendix 2), complementarity with knowledge distillation (Table 5), additional datasets (Pascal VOC, BDD100K; Table 11), and ablation studies on teacher backbone (Table 3) and prior choice (Table 10).

The paper honestly and quantitatively addresses the computational overhead of the pre-scoring stage (Table 12) and demonstrates that the method reaches comparable performance in substantially fewer iterations (Fig. 9: ~52% iterations), and that gains persist under longer schedules where the baseline overfits (Table 13), strengthening the practical case.

Combining DetGain with strong online data augmentation is a sensible and empirically validated design choice (Table 2), and the observation that pure learnability sampling collapses into a narrow subspace causing overfitting is well-argued and supported.

The writing is clear, the motivation for the metric-driven (rather than loss-driven) signal is well articulated, and the supplementary material provides comprehensive implementation details (Algorithm 1, augmentation table, polynomial weight lookup).
weaknesses: The per-iteration wall-clock overhead is substantial (~200% in Table 12: 0.25s to 0.75s), and while fewer iterations are needed, the net benefit depends heavily on training length and hardware. A more explicit end-to-end wall-clock comparison (accounting for the reduced iterations) would strengthen the efficiency claims, though Table 13 and Fig. 9 partially address this.

The uniform prior Beta(1,1) simplification, while elegant and shown to preserve ranking (Fig. 4, Appendix 6), discards detector-specific score distributions. The paper acknowledges validation AP is essentially unchanged (Table 10) but the theoretical justification for why the uniform prior is nearly lossless in ranking is somewhat post-hoc.

The method requires a pretrained teacher model, which adds training cost and infrastructure overhead. Although Appendix 1 shows same-family teachers work best, this reduces the 'no extra data' claim and adds a dependency that pure single-model methods avoid.

The reported gains, while consistent, are moderate (~2.0 mAP on COCO across detectors), and the largest gains come from noise/pseudo-label regimes. It is not fully clear how much of the improvement stems from the metric-aware score versus the strong augmentation and larger effective sampling diversity; the ablation in Table 2 helps but the decomposition could be sharper.

The method operates on post-processed detections and uses a first-order additive approximation for the image-level aggregation (Eq. 27); while the authors argue the remainder is negligible when |B| << |D|, the interaction effects of joint insertion (e.g., two informative images competing for the same TP) are not empirically bounded on the full dataset.

Reproducibility would be improved by a statement about code/model release, which is not mentioned; the polynomial surrogate coefficients and augmentation probabilities are given but their tuning procedure is not fully detailed.

The core teacher-student learnability concept is adapted from prior work (e.g., RHO-LOSS, JEST); the primary novelty is the mAP-aligned metric reformulation and its closed-form derivation, which is a solid but incremental conceptual extension to the detection domain.

strengths: Well-motivated problem framing: the paper correctly identifies that loss-based learnability signals are unreliable for object detection because detection losses are fragmented (classification, localization, centerness), depend on stochastic proposal sampling and assignment rules (RPN/Hungarian matching), and drift across iterations. Replacing these with a metric-aligned, dataset-level mAP signal is a sensible and original angle for online curation in detection.

The mathematical core is carefully developed and verified. The derivation of the marginal AP change for TP and FP insertion (Eqs. 18-20 and the closed forms in Eqs. 25-26 under a uniform Beta(1,1) prior) is non-trivial, and the Monte Carlo verification in Fig. 7 shows the analytic solution matches simulation almost exactly, giving confidence in the estimator. The O(1) per-detection scoring cost makes online use plausible.

Strong empirical breadth: DetGain is evaluated on six representative detectors spanning two-stage (Faster R-CNN), anchor-based one-stage (ATSS, GFL), anchor-free (FCOS, VFNet), and transformer-based (Deformable DETR) families, with consistent improvements (~+2.0 mAP average) and reported variance over three seeds. Additional evidence on Pascal VOC and BDD100K (Table 11) supports generalization across dataset scales and distributions.

Thorough and honest ablations: the necessity of combining sampling with strong augmentation (Table 2, Fig. 3), the effect of teacher backbone capacity (Table 3), the uniform-prior vs. detector-specific prior comparison (Fig. 4, Table 10), the longer-schedule study that rules out gains being a trivial artifact of extra compute (Table 13), and the runtime/memory breakdown (Table 12) collectively address many natural reviewer questions.

Robustness studies are a genuine plus: controlled annotation noise (Fig. 5), pseudo-label training with YOLOv8-generated labels (Table 7), and complementarity with knowledge distillation (Table 5) demonstrate practical value beyond a single clean benchmark. The plug-and-play, model-agnostic claim is well supported since only the data pipeline is modified.

The paper is clearly written and largely reproducible: implementation details (MMDetection, schedules, super-batch size, selection ratio), algorithmic pseudo-code (Algorithm 1), and the augmentation configuration (Table 9) are provided.
weaknesses: The computational overhead is significant and somewhat understated by the 'minimally intrusive' framing. Table 12 shows +200% per-iteration wall-clock time for the naive implementation (0.25s to 0.75s), with non-data time increasing from 0.22s to 0.68s. Even the dynamic selection ratio only reduces this to ~30% extra training time. Given that data curation is often motivated by compute savings, the net efficiency trade-off deserves more candid discussion and comparison (e.g., cost-per-unit-accuracy vs. simply training longer or on more data).

There is a potential confound between strong data augmentation and DetGain sampling. Table 2 shows augmentation alone barely helps validation (37.5 vs. 37.4 baseline) while augmentation + sampling reaches 39.9, which is a good disentanglement; however, in Table 1 the reported '+DetGain' deltas are measured against the baseline rather than against the '+Data Aug' column, so the augmentation contribution is folded into the headline numbers. The isolation could be presented more transparently.

The central premise—that a sample's individual marginal contribution to dataset-level mAP is the right quantity to rank for training value—is ultimately a heuristic. A single image's DetGain is computed under a first-order additive approximation and a uniform score prior, and the paper does not establish a theoretical link between ranking by this quantity and improved optimization. The empirical gains support the heuristic, but the argument that this is a principled 'contribution to AP' is weaker than presented.

The comparison set in Table 4 (gradient norm, hard mining, entropy, image-wise AP, loss-learnability) is reasonable, but it is not clear these baselines were tuned as carefully as DetGain, and the margins are modest in several cells (e.g., Faster R-CNN AP 40.0 vs. 38.9 for loss-learnability). A comparison against a modern online coreset/active-learning baseline under the same augmented super-batch protocol would strengthen the claim of superiority.

Although variance is reported, no statistical significance testing is performed, and the absolute gains (~+2 mAP, with some cells only +1.6 to +1.8) are meaningful but not large. The relative advantage over strong learnability baselines is sometimes within overlapping error bars, which slightly tempers the strength of the claims.

The uniform-prior simplification deliberately discards detector-specific score distributions; the paper argues (via Spearman ~0.94, Fig. 4) that ranking is preserved, but the absolute DetGain values are acknowledged to be approximate. This limits interpretability of the score itself and means the method's behavior depends on a ranking-only justification that is empirically, not analytically, supported.

strengths: The central idea is well motivated and non-trivial: instead of adapting loss-based 'learnability' (which is demonstrably unstable in detection because classification/localization losses are fragmented and perturbed by RPN sampling, Hungarian matching and NMS), the paper defines an image-level score as its marginal contribution to the *evaluation metric*, dataset-level mAP. The diagnosis of why generic data-selection metrics transfer poorly to detection (Sec. 1, Sec. 2.1) is accurate and the fix is principled.

There is a real technical contribution in Sec. 3.2 and Appendix A3: writing (non-interpolated) AP as a Stieltjes integral, decomposing the single-insertion ΔAP into a self-contribution and a precision-reweighting term (Eqs. 13-20), and deriving closed forms under a uniform Beta(1,1) score prior (Eqs. 25-26). The derivation is careful, the Monte-Carlo verification in Fig. 7 shows essentially exact agreement with simulation for both TP and FP insertion across several detector priors, and the ranking-stability study (Fig. 4, Spearman 0.94; Fig. 6, Spearman ≈1 as |D| grows) gives reasonable support for the additive/ranking surrogate.

The method is genuinely architecture-agnostic and minimally intrusive: it consumes only standard post-processed outputs (boxes, scores, labels, IoUs) and is evaluated across two-stage (Faster R-CNN), anchor-based one-stage (ATSS, GFL), anchor-free (FCOS, VFNet) and transformer (Deformable DETR) detectors — a broader cross-architecture study than is typical for online-sampling papers, and a practical advantage over RoI/anchor-level schemes such as ATSS or Focal Loss.

The empirical evidence is broad: Table 1 (6 detectors, 3 seeds), Table 4 (comparison against uniform, hard mining, GradNorm, class entropy, entropy+diversity, image-AP and loss-learnability), Table 5 (KD complementarity), Table 11 (VOC +3.0, BDD100K +1.8), Fig. 5 (annotation-noise robustness) and Table 7 (pseudo-labels). Improvements over the +Data Aug baseline are consistent (+1.6 to +2.9 mAP) and the gains over the strongest competing sampling metric (loss-learnability) are +1.1/+2.8/+1.2 on the three Table 4 detectors.

Several ablations are honest and informative rather than flattering: Table 2 reports that online sampling *alone* degrades validation accuracy (37.3 vs 37.4) and causes severe train/val divergence; Table 3 quantifies the teacher-backbone effect; Table 10 shows the fitted model-specific prior does not beat the uniform prior on validation; Fig. 9 shows Deformable DETR reaching the baseline's best mAP in ~52% of iterations and Table 13 shows the baseline saturating/overfitting at long schedules while DetGain keeps improving. Reporting these negative/limiting results increases trust in the rest.
weaknesses: The efficiency case is weak and partly contradicts the abstract's framing. Table 12 reports +200% per-iteration wall-clock (0.25s → 0.75s) for the naive implementation on Faster R-CNN-R50, because the 80-image super-batch requires extra forward passes plus stronger augmentation (data time 26.3 → 72.6 ms). The main results in Table 1 are therefore not compute-matched against the baseline: DetGain gets 5x the forward passes and a hand-tuned augmentation pool per iteration. The claim that the method 'reduces total training time by ~30% in practice' rests on a single Deformable-DETR iteration-count curve (Fig. 9, dynamic k schedule in Appendix 8) and is not supported in wall-clock terms for the detectors in Table 1. Table 13 partly addresses schedule-matched comparison but does not resolve the compute-fairness issue.

The method's benefit is inseparable from a large, loosely specified augmentation pipeline. Table 2 shows that without strong augmentation, DetGain subsampling is worse than the baseline on validation (37.3 vs 37.4) with massive overfitting (train 50.3). The augmentation component (Table 9: ~25 operators, family-specific probabilities that are 'roughly adjusted', Copy-Paste, etc.) is substantial and its tuning is not ablated or described precisely enough to separate its contribution from the sampler's. The reported gains are joint effects of sampler + augmentation recipe.

Attribution and framing overstate the results. The abstract and Fig. 1 quote +2.7 mAP and Fig. 1's +2.18/+2.52/+2.63 relative to a *plain* baseline that receives no augmentation, whereas the apples-to-apples comparison (vs +Data Aug) is +1.6 to +2.9 mAP. The '+6.9 mAP on low-quality data' figure is taken at the 100% noise level where all methods collapse (Fig. 5), a degenerate regime. The claim of 'the first data-efficient online curation pipeline' for detection is too strong given RHO-LOSS/JEST/ACED and the AP-driven image-level selection of Zhou et al. [62] acknowledged in Sec. 2.1.

The two key approximations are validated only in simulation, not in the training loop. The per-image additivity assumption (Eqs. 9, 27) and the uniform Beta(1,1) prior discard the model's actual score/IoU distributions and all cross-sample interactions; support comes from synthetic Spearman-rank checks (Fig. 4, Fig. 6). No experiment selects samples with a deliberately mis-specified prior or a known interaction-heavy setting to bound the failure mode, so the claim that 'relative ordering is preserved' remains an assumption for real training dynamics.

Marginal novelty relative to the closest prior work. The teacher-student 'learnability' formulation is from RHO-LOSS [38] and the AP-driven image-level selection signal from [62]; the new elements are the dataset-level (rather than image-level) marginal-AP estimator and its closed form. That is a legitimate but incremental step, and the measured advantage over the closest competitor (loss-learnability, +1.1 to +2.8 mAP on 3 detectors) is modest.

Reproducibility and setup transparency. No code release is stated. The teacher is trained on the same training set, so the signal reflects capacity/optimization gaps rather than new information, and the additional teacher training/inference cost is never accounted for. The per-image TP/FP matching convention (only the highest-scoring TP per GT) appears only in Appendix 8, and augmentation probabilities are described qualitatively, making exact reproduction difficult.

Presentation issues: numerous typos and inconsistencies ('HTgh-quality' in the abstract, 'DeteGain'/'GAPs-learngability' in Fig. 2 and Algorithm 1, 'stable monotonic', inconsistent use of ΔAP/δ_AP and DetGain/δ_DG). Individually minor, but together with the mismatched headline numbers they make the paper harder to trust at a glance.
